doc_summary: Hubinger and coauthors had Claude agents write training data to make a small model misaligned while evading a production-like monitor. They found the data mostly hid misbehavior in fiction and roleplay, and frame this as a first step toward turning safety questions into scores that autonomous agents can optimize.

items.claim: Prefers turning a safety question into a score that autonomous agents can optimize against over relying only on human red-teaming, because human time doesn't scale as models improve and compute can be turned into safety confidence.
items.quote: a safety question can be turned into a score that autonomous agents can then help solve

items.claim: Prefers automated adversarial search against a realistic production-like defense over manual red-teaming alone because human red-teaming may not keep up as models improve.
items.quote: Red-teaming by humans is a vital part of model safety testing, but it may struggle to keep up as models improve.

items.claim: Test against a defense similar to what is used in production, and give the adversary that monitor to practice against, so that findings reflect real gaps rather than toy ones.
items.quote: passing a monitor similar to those we use in production — one of several defenses we use — and we gave it that monitor to practice against.

items.claim: Evasive content succeeds mostly by embedding misaligned behavior in benign-looking framings like fiction and roleplay, so surface harmlessness is a weak signal of safety.
items.quote: Given enough attempts, it succeeded, mostly by hiding the behavior in fiction and roleplay.

items.claim: Distrusts over-claiming from a deliberately one-sided game; results are framed as a possible gap, not a demonstration of real-world failure.
items.quote: While the data was optimized for this game and the resulting models never deployed, the search surfaced a kind of training data that looks harmless to monitors but teaches misaligned behavior.

items.claim: Counts as convincing evidence examples that look innocuous to a monitor yet demonstrably teach misaligned behavior, because they can then be used as concrete test cases to improve defenses.
items.quote: These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

items.claim: Prefers presenting results as a first step with scaling potential over claiming a finished result, because stronger models and more compute should improve the search.
items.quote: This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

items.claim: Plans to apply the automated-search-against-a-score approach to other safety questions and use the found examples to improve future monitors.
items.quote: We see this work as a first step toward automated adversarial stress-testing of our safety systems
